summary:
Selangor stands under Malaysia's national framework. Sections 377A to 377D of the federal Penal Code punish same-sex intimacy and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment and whipping; the provisions apply regardless of gender, reach conduct regardless of consent, and have been enforced in recent years. They are not limited to Malaysian citizens, so a foreign visitor is exposed to them.

Layered on top, every one of Malaysia's 13 states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintains Sharia enactments criminalising cross-dressing or a man posing as a woman, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These offences reach Muslims only, so a non-Muslim visitor does not fall under them.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without touching the federal one. In February 2021 the Federal Court struck down provisions of Selangor's Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 as exceeding the state's legislative power. The Penal Code offences remained fully intact, and a High Court request to declare the Sharia cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional had earlier been denied.

Selangor is where Malaysia's religious-enforcement apparatus has been most publicly directed at gender expression. In 2021 Nur Sajat, a transgender woman and cosmetics entrepreneur, failed to appear in a Selangor Syariah court to answer charges of "insulting Islam" grounded in her attire. The state religious department issued a warrant for her arrest and announced that 122 religious-affairs officers had been mobilised to hunt her down, then sought her extradition from Thailand. She was allowed to remain under UNHCR protection and later settled in Australia.

Arrests for gender nonconformity and same-sex conduct are pursued through raids and venue-based operations rather than individual stops. A Selangor Syariah court sentenced five men to six or seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane. Investigations of the kind documented by Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters covered Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah, showing a nationwide pattern of which Selangor is one data point.

State "rehabilitation" programmes have drawn at least 1,733 participants as of June 2021, within a crackdown on LGBT people running since the 2018 election; the programmes were found to internalise discrimination and foster self-hatred among attendees.

Violence against trans people in Selangor has been lethal. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in under two months, and documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor the practical exposure is the Penal Code, not the Sharia enactments. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely singled out; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest followed by public outing, with media pre-tipped and detainees' identities leaked.
tangentialFactors:
Selangor's enforcement sits inside a wider regional pattern. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister stated that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his full licence to carry out enforcement against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B in the largest operation of its kind since 2022; detainees' faces and personal details were leaked, 17 civil servants among them were suspended, and more than 130 people were held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet release was delayed. Days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

On 8 June 2014, 16 trans women were arrested en masse at a wedding, and a constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014. In February 2024 the Federal Court struck down 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions on federalism grounds, the same reasoning used against Selangor's section 28 in 2021.

The surrounding climate constrains reform: Islamist opposition has foreclosed changes to the Penal Code, LGBT events and media content are censored, there is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters released their joint report on state-backed discrimination on 10 August 2022.
localsOnly:
Malaysians who are Muslim face a two-tier criminal regime. The federal Penal Code applies to everyone, and the state Sharia enactments add cross-dressing and gender-nonconformity offences enforced by state Islamic religious departments; three of the 13 states also bar women from posing as men. The Sharia laws contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing, leaving the standard to the enforcing officer.

Since the 1980s all 13 states have passed such enactments. Selangor's version was cut back by the Federal Court in 2021, but residents remain exposed to the federal offences and to whatever provisions of the Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 survived.

State "rehabilitation" and mukhayyam retreats are offered as an alternative to prosecution: at least 1,733 people had attended by June 2021, and assessments found the programmes internalise discrimination and foment self-hatred. There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination law and no same-sex marriage, and LGBT events and media content are censored.

Residents have limited recourse after arrest. Documentation of the 2019 Klang killing records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself". Justice For Sisters has mobilised bailors and legal aid in response to mass arrests, and on 2 December 2025 the Home Minister floated revisiting section 377.
